'''''Calculus on Manifolds: A Modern Approach to Classical Theorems of Advanced Calculus''''' (1965) by [[Michael Spivak]] is a brief, rigorous, and modern textbook on multivariable calculus, differential forms, and integration on manifolds for advanced undergraduates.

==Description==
''Calculus on Manifolds'' is a brief [[monograph]] on  the [[Real analysis|theory]] of vector-valued functions of [[Multivariable calculus|several real variables]] (<math>f: \mathbb{R}^n \mapsto \mathbb{R}^m</math>) and [[differentiable manifold]]s in Euclidean space. In addition to extending the concepts of [[Differentiation (calculus)|differentiation]] (including the [[Inverse function theorem|inverse]] and [[implicit function theorem]]s) and [[Riemann integration]] (including [[Fubini's theorem]]) to functions of several variables, the book treats the classical theorems of vector calculus, including those of [[Green's theorem|Green]], [[Gauss' theorem|Gauss]], and [[Stokes' theorem|Stokes]], in the language of [[differential form]]s on [[differentiable manifold]]s embedded in [[Euclidean space]], and as [[Corollary|corollaries]] of the [[generalized Stokes theorem]] on [[Manifold#Manifold with boundary|manifolds with boundaries]].  The book culminates with the statement and proof of this vast and abstract modern generalization of several classical results:{{efn|The formalisms of differential forms and the exterior calculus used in ''Calculus on Manifolds'' were first formulated by [[Élie Cartan]].  Using this language, Cartan stated the generalized Stokes' theorem in its modern form, publishing the simple, elegant formula shown here in 1945.  For a detailed discussion of how Stokes' theorem developed historically, see {{Harvtxt|Katz|1979|pp=146–156}}.}}

{{math_theorem
| name = Stokes' Theorem for Manifolds with Boundaries.|''If'' <math>M</math> ''is a compact oriented'' <math>k</math>''-dimensional manifold-with-boundary,'' <math>\partial M</math> ''is the boundary given the induced orientation, and'' <math>\omega</math> ''is a'' (<math>k-1</math>)''-form on'' <math>M</math>'', then'' <math>\int_M d\omega =\int_{\partial M} \omega</math>.
}}

The cover of ''Calculus on Manifolds'' features snippets of a July 2, 1850 letter from [[Lord Kelvin]] to Sir [[Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet|George Stokes]] containing the first disclosure of the classical Stokes' theorem.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Spivak|2018|p=viii}}</ref>

==Reception==
''Calculus on Manifolds'' aims to present the topics of [[Multivariable calculus|multivariable]] and [[vector calculus]] in the manner in which they are seen by a modern working mathematician, yet simply and selectively enough to be understood by undergraduate students whose previous coursework in mathematics comprises only single-variable calculus and introductory linear algebra. While Spivak's elementary treatment of modern mathematical tools is broadly successful—and this approach has made ''Calculus on Manifolds'' a standard introduction to the rigorous theory of multivariable calculus—the text is also well known for its laconic style, lack of motivating examples, and frequent omission of non-obvious steps and arguments.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/calculus-on-manifolds-a-modern-approach-to-classical-theorems-of-advanced-calculus |date=2007-06-15 |last=Gouvêa |first=Fernando Q. |title=Calculus on Manifolds: A Modern Approach to Classical Theorems of Advanced Calculus {{!}} Mathematical Association of America |website=www.maa.org |access-date=2017-04-09}}</ref><ref>{{Harvtxt|Munkres|1968}}</ref> For example, in order to state and prove the generalized Stokes' theorem on chains, a profusion of unfamiliar concepts and constructions (e.g., [[Multilinear form|tensor products]], differential forms, [[tangent space]]s, [[Pullback (differential geometry)|pullbacks]], [[exterior derivative]]s, [[Chain (algebraic topology)|cube and chains]]) are introduced in quick succession within the span of 25 pages.  Moreover, careful readers have noted a number of nontrivial oversights throughout the text, including missing hypotheses in theorems, inaccurately stated theorems, and proofs that fail to handle all cases.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jirka.org/spivak-errata.html|title=Spivak - Calculus on Manifolds -- Comments and Errata|last=Lebl|first=Jiří}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.petraaxolotl.com/mathematics/Calculus-on-Manifolds/|title=Calculus on Manifolds Errata|last=Axolotl|first=Petra|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110060222/http://www.petraaxolotl.com/mathematics/Calculus-on-Manifolds/|archive-date=2017-01-10|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/206145 |title=Error in the statement of Thm. 2-13 in Calculus on Manifolds|author=koletenbert|date=2012-10-02}}</ref>

==Other textbooks==
A more recent textbook which also covers these topics at an undergraduate level is the text ''Analysis on Manifolds'' (1991) by [[James Munkres]].<ref>{{Harvtxt|Munkres|1991}}</ref> At 366 pages or more than twice the length of ''Calculus on Manifolds'', Munkres's work presents a more careful and detailed treatment of the subject matter at a leisurely pace.  Nevertheless, Munkres acknowledges the influence of Spivak's earlier text in the preface of his text.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Munkres|1991|p=vii}}</ref>

Spivak's five-volume textbook ''A Comprehensive Introduction to Differential Geometry'' states in its preface that ''Calculus on Manifolds'' serves as a prerequisite for a course based on this text.  In fact, several of the concepts introduced in ''Calculus on Manifolds'' reappear in the first volume of this classic work in more sophisticated settings.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Spivak|1999}}</ref>
